name: Choosing a Vector Store
question: Which vector database should we actually run?
summary: Choosing a vector store is a product decision, not an algorithm choice: the index types covered elsewhere in this module (IVF, HNSW, DiskANN) are available in most stores. The options fall into four families: a vector extension in a database you already run (Postgres with pgvector), a dedicated open-source engine (Qdrant, Milvus, Weaviate), a managed serverless service (Pinecone and others) and an existing search engine (OpenSearch, Elasticsearch). The deciding constraints are usually scale, filtering and hybrid needs, where the data must live, how much operations time the team has, and cost at your size. Shortlist on those, then benchmark two finalists on your own data and queries.
useCases: Starting a first RAG or search product
A data residency or audit requirement that rules options in or out

steps: Write down scale, filters, residency, latency target and ops budget
Shortlist two families that meet every hard constraint
Benchmark both on a sample of real documents and queries, with filters
Choose, and keep an export path: vectors and metadata in an open format
pitfalls: Choosing from a public benchmark that used different data, filters and hardware
Adding a new database when Postgres with pgvector would have served for years
Ignoring where the data must live until a compliance review blocks launch
remember: Constraints first, two finalists, benchmark on your own queries.

steps.title: Write the constraints down
steps.text: Suvidha Finance, a fictional NBFC, has 1 crore chunks, expects 3× growth in two years, wants p95 under 50 ms, needs filters and hybrid search, and must keep vectors in its own cloud account. The team can spare about 20 operations hours a month.

steps.title: Shortlist on hard constraints
steps.text: A managed serverless store in the vendor’s account fails the residency rule, so it is out before any benchmark. pgvector, a self-hosted engine and the existing OpenSearch cluster remain.

steps.title: Benchmark on your own data
steps.text: Load a real sample with its metadata and replay 1,000 logged queries with their filters. Public benchmarks use other data and hardware.

steps.title: Measure what you will pay for
steps.text: Record recall at 10, p95 latency, monthly cost and operations hours for each finalist.

steps.title: Decide
steps.text: At 1 crore, pgvector’s p95 is 60 ms; a self-hosted Qdrant cluster gives 20 ms for ₹40,000 a month and about 16 operations hours. It meets every constraint.

steps.title: Keep an exit
steps.text: Export ids, vectors, metadata and ACLs nightly in an open format, so a later move is a reload, not a rewrite.

pros: Hard constraints remove most options before any benchmark
Your own queries reveal filter and hybrid behaviour public tests miss
Staying in Postgres avoids a new system when it is enough
An export path keeps the choice reversible
cons: A fair benchmark takes days of setup
Costs change with vendor pricing and your growth
Self-hosting shifts on-call and upgrades to your team
Managed services may not meet residency rules
avoidWhen: Running two new databases because each team chose its own

library.name: pgvector
library.what: Vector columns and HNSW indexes inside Postgres, often the right first store.

practice.note: This script benchmarks one finalist (pgvector). Write the same small adapter for the second finalist and run the same queries. Table and column names are examples.

samples.code:
import json, time, statistics, numpy as np, psycopg
from pgvector.psycopg import register_vector

conn = psycopg.connect("dbname=search", autocommit=True)
register_vector(conn)
queries = [json.loads(l) for l in open("queries_with_truth.jsonl")]   # vec, branch, truth_ids

lat, hits = [], 0
for q in queries:
    t = time.perf_counter()
    rows = conn.execute(
        "SELECT id FROM chunks WHERE branch = %s ORDER BY embedding <=> %s LIMIT 10",
        (q["branch"], np.array(q["vec"]))).fetchall()
    lat.append((time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000)
    hits += len({r[0] for r in rows} & set(q["truth_ids"]))

print("recall@10", round(hits / (10 * len(queries)), 3))
print("p95 ms", round(statistics.quantiles(lat, n=20)[18], 1))

numericDrill.question: A self-hosted engine costs ₹40,000 a month plus 16 operations hours at ₹1,500 an hour. A managed store costs ₹55,000 plus 2 hours. How many ₹ a month cheaper is the cheaper option?
numericDrill.answer: Self-hosted: 40,000 + 16 × 1,500 = ₹64,000. Managed: 55,000 + 2 × 1,500 = ₹58,000. Managed is ₹6,000 a month cheaper.

interview.question: How would you choose a vector database?
interview.answer: Write down hard constraints (scale, filters and hybrid, data residency, operations budget, cost), shortlist two options that meet them, benchmark both on your own data and logged queries with filters, and keep an export path.

interview.question: When is pgvector enough?
interview.answer: When you already run Postgres and the corpus is up to roughly a crore of vectors with moderate query load; you keep joins, transactions and one system to operate.
